title: Reporting and representation of population descriptors in public RNA-seq databases.
data_url: https://figshare.unimelb.edu.au/projects/RNA-seq_diversity/221698 (raw deposit, 2 items) and https://doi.org/10.26188/32843678 (code + processed_data, CC BY-NC 4.0); supplementary tables via Europe PMC PMC13576982

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC search on the DOI returned exactly 1 hit (PMID 42594880, PMC13576982, open access, licence CC BY-NC). I downloaded the full-text XML (168,170 bytes) and read the Summary, all six Results subsections, Table 1, 'Data and code availability', the Key resources table, every STAR Methods subsection and 'Limitations of the study'. (1) Figshare application programming interface: project 221698 'RNA-seq diversity' contains exactly two items - dbGaP_study_649.csv (577,100 bytes, CC BY 4.0) and 'SRA metadata - 11Mar24.zip' (83,596,712 bytes, CC BY-NC 4.0). (2) I downloaded and opened dbGaP_study_649.csv with pandas: 649 rows x 16 columns, columns accession / name / description / Parent study / Study Disease-Focus / Study Design / Study Markerset / Study Molecular Data Type / Study Content / Ancestry (computed) / NIH Institute / Study Consent / Release Date / Embargo Release Date / Related Terms / Collections. Every one is study-level free text or a comma-separated blob; 'Ancestry (computed)' is 94.5% empty and 'Collections' 67.6% empty; dates are US-style strings such as '4/17/24'. (3) The 83.6 MB SRA metadata zip is over my 50 MB download rule, so I did not download it; instead I read its central directory by HTTP range request on the last 70,000 bytes. It holds 81 entries totalling about 1.1 gigabytes uncompressed, all of it raw NCBI SRA Run Selector metadata dumps (8Sep23_run_selector_metadata.txt 61,059,509 bytes; the post-2019 companion 143,322,786 bytes; 31 SraRunTable_*.txt; five sra_result_*.csv up to 64,643,688 bytes) plus one README.docx. I then fetched only the README.docx member (10,683 compressed bytes) by byte range and inflated it locally. (4) I downloaded the code deposit, RNAseq_diversity.zip, 21,407,858 bytes, md5 394e4be89aaeef31e699323f621a6dff matching the Figshare record. It is a 2026-07-01 freeze of github.com/AmandaJLea/RNAseq_diversity: 13 R Markdown analysis files with rendered HTML, a README that is still the unedited GitLab template (no documentation at all), and a processed_data folder with four files. (5) Using R's readRDS I opened 20240901_allSRAFinal_for_plotting.rds: 23,880 rows x 51 columns, 23,880 distinct BioSample accessions, 261 distinct SRA study accessions. Columns I read include the eight raw descriptor fields (ETHNICITY, RACE, Population, ancestry, DONOR_ETHNICITY, reported_race, race.ethnicity, primary_race) and the harmonised outputs (finalRace, finalGeography, hispanic, strictestRace, strictestGeography, strictRace, strictGeography, backupRace, worldBank, worldRegion, hasDescriptor). Counts I computed myself: hasDescriptor = Racial 14,055 / Geographic 9,825; finalRace = White 12,538, missing 7,083, Black or African American 2,993, Asian 658, Other 278, Multiple 244, American Indian or Alaskan Native 67, Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander 19; finalGeography = missing 17,184, Europe 3,281, East Asia 1,333, South Asia 773, Subsaharan Africa 524, Asia 304, Multiple 206, Americas 164, Southeast Asia 83, North Africa and Western Asia 27, Other 1; finalCountry = USA 14,804 of 23,880; ReleaseDate spans 2012-2022; median 32 samples per study, maximum 1,857; no duplicated BioSample; donor_id is filled for only 420 rows (260 distinct donors), so repeated measures on the same person are mostly untraceable. The decisive count: pasting together the eight raw descriptor fields gives only 308 distinct input strings across all 23,880 rows, and just 3 of those 308 strings map to more than one harmonised label. (6) I opened the manual-review export, which is deposited under the literal filename 'C:\combinedRecount3.csv' (a Windows path baked into the file name): 678 rows x 193 columns, a Google-Form dump; 620 distinct recount3 study identifiers with 58 deliberate repeat reviews; 'Include study?' = Yes 376 / No 258 / Unsure 44; 'Does the study report any of the following' = nothing reported 291, Race 31, Ethnicity 17, Ancestry 15, Race+Ethnicity 5, missing 314; 12 reviewer initials with casing inconsistencies (GNR and gnr, RPR and RP); the 193 columns are the same 25-column block repeated for up to eight sample types, and blocks 2-8 are 90-99.7% empty. (7) 20240731_dbgap_final.rds is 324 rows x 15 columns; 20240916_manual_final.rds is 120 rows x 14 columns. (8) I grepped the R Markdown files for their inputs: they read 20250605_allSRAFilt_country.rds, 20250517_allSRAFinal.rds, from_Kasper_suppTable3.csv, final_bioproject_biosample_runlist.csv and SRA_metadata/*.txt, none of which are in the deposit - so the published analysis cannot be re-run end to end, and the one sample-level table that is deposited is a 2024-09-01 snapshot predating the 2025 revision. (9) I downloaded the Europe PMC supplementary bundle (17,143,129 bytes, 20 files) and opened all five spreadsheets with pandas: mmc2.xlsx = Table S1 World Bank country groups (270 x 4); mmc3.xlsx = Table S2 United Nations country populations (240 x 3); mmc4.xlsx = Table S4 'Recoding of population descriptor categories and terms from SRA', 454 data rows x 8 columns (Term / Frequency / Original SRA category / Harmonised recoding (Hispanic) / Harmonised recoding (category) / Harmonised recoding (term) / two alternative-coding columns); mmc5.xlsx = Table S9 tissue recoding (968 x 8, carrying Cell Ontology and UBERON anatomy identifiers); mmc6.xlsx = Table S10 disease recoding (279 x 7, carrying Disease Ontology identifiers). On Table S4 I computed: 271 distinct (Term, Original SRA category) keys, and exactly 0 of them map to more than one harmonised term - it is a perfect lookup table. 183 of the 454 terms (frequency sum 10,756) have no harmonised term at all, because they are junk such as 'human', 'Bulk', 'R11', 'Not available' or cell-sorting gates. The Frequency column sums to 36,427. I also noticed the internal spreadsheet sheet names are mislabelled relative to the printed table numbers (the sheet named 'Table S6' holds Table S4; 'Table S4' holds Table S2; 'Table S10' holds Table S9; 'Table S11' holds Table S10).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the full SRA denominator and about genetic ancestry. From Table 1 and the Results, read but not verifiable from any deposited file: 12,293 SRA studies and 747,964 BioSamples passing filters, of which 23,803 (3%) carry any population descriptor, split 9,803 geographic and 14,000 US Census, from 244 studies; 55% of samples deposited by United States institutions and 90% by institutions in high-income countries; 69.1% of US Census-labelled samples labelled White (9,669/14,000); 56% of geographic-labelled samples labelled European (5,451/9,803); 649 dbGaP studies with 167,389 individuals of whom 47,022 have a GrafPop-derived ancestry assignment; 105,966 SRA BioSamples with a genetically inferred continental label taken from Razi et al., of which only 3,176 also have an author-provided geographic descriptor, and 729 of those called European by the author but 1000 Genomes admixed-American-like by genotype; the literature review yielding 312 usable studies and 16,801 individuals, with 61/312 studies reporting any descriptor and only 3 of those 61 also depositing it in SRA; and all the over-representation statistics (United States overrepresented 14.6-fold, Europe-labelled 3.6-fold in SRA and 4.04-fold in dbGaP, Fisher odds ratio 6.03 for US versus non-US term choice, and the non-significant year correlations r = 0.09 to 0.35). I did not open mmc1.pdf (Document S1, 6,832,957 bytes, holding Methods S1, Figures S1-S16 and Tables S3, S5-S8, S11, S12), mmc7.pdf (peer review) or mmc8.pdf (article), so everything in Tables S3 and S5-S8 is paper-text-only for me. I also did not retrieve the Razi et al. supplementary table that carries the genetic ancestry labels and principal components; it is not in this paper's deposit.

a1_downloadable.note: Passes. Everything is genuinely open: no login, no access application, no embargo. I pulled the Figshare records through the public application programming interface, downloaded the 577 KB dbGaP table and the 21 MB code archive (md5 matched the record), and got all 20 supplementary files from Europe PMC. One friction, not a failure: the 83.6 MB raw SRA metadata zip exceeds my own 50 MB download rule, so I listed its contents by HTTP range request instead and pulled only its 13 KB README.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAILS. Nothing in these files is a measurement of anything. Every column is either a string a depositor typed into an optional metadata field, or a category the authors assigned to that string by hand. The only target with a physical basis - the actual genetic ancestry of the donor - is absent: it lives in Razi et al.'s separate supplementary table, and the merged table the paper used (3,176 samples with both an author label and a genetic label) was never deposited, so you would have to rebuild it yourself from two sources with a one-to-many Run-to-BioSample join. That is the textbook 'you would have to build the thing you are predicting'.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAILS for the only framing with a real measurement behind it. If the task is 'infer a donor's genetic ancestry from their RNA sequencing data', the inputs are present only as BioSample accession numbers (SAMN...); the actual expression or read data sits in recount3 and the Sequence Read Archive across 747,964 samples, which is hundreds of thousands of lookups and terabytes of download. For the much weaker text framing the input is present, but it is a single short string per row and there are only 308 distinct ones.

a4_units_stated.note: Passes trivially, because nothing here is a physical quantity needing units - every field is a category, a count of samples, or a date. Two small traps I did see in the files: the dbGaP table's Release Date is an ambiguous US-style string ('4/17/24'), and the manual-review form's many 'Number of individuals' columns are counts with no stated denominator, which the authors themselves name as a source of reviewer disagreement.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS, in the 'big number, tiny effective n' way. The sample table has 23,880 rows, but I counted only 308 distinct input strings in it, from 261 studies - and the string is the entire input, so the real number of independent examples is 308, far under the checklist's 400 floor even for pure classification. The other deposited tables are smaller still: 649 dbGaP studies, 678 manual-review rows covering 620 studies of which only about 61 report any descriptor at all, 324 and 120 rows in the two summary files.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: about 1.4 MB for everything you would actually model (the 23,880-row table, the 649-row dbGaP table, the 678-row review export and the 454-row recoding dictionary); 83.6 MB compressed / about 1.1 GB uncompressed if you ever wanted the raw Run Selector dumps
a6_fits_laptop.note: Passes comfortably and is the one place this resource scores well. Peak memory to load every deposited table at once is well under a gigabyte, and no graphics card is involved. Reading the raw metadata dumps would mean streaming roughly 1.1 GB of tab-separated text one file at a time, which is routine.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: FAILS, though this is the mildest of the failures. Four different totals exist for the same quantity: the published Table 1 says 23,803 descriptor-bearing BioSamples (9,803 geographic + 14,000 US Census) from 244 studies; the deposited table I opened has 23,880 rows (9,825 Geographic + 14,055 Racial) from 261 studies; the Methods text says 9,375 + 13,038 + 1,011 before de-duplication; and Table S4's Frequency column sums to 36,427 descriptor entries. The likely cause is visible in the code - the R Markdown files read 20250517_allSRAFinal.rds and 20250605_allSRAFilt_country.rds, which are not in the deposit, so the only sample-level file released is a 2024-09-01 snapshot from before the revision. I can explain the gap but I cannot tell which numbers are right from the files.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAILS decisively, and this is the clearest failure of the eight. The harmonised label (finalRace, finalGeography, strictestRace, strictestGeography) is produced by applying the published 454-row recoding table in supplementary Table S4 to the raw descriptor string. I checked that table myself: 271 distinct (term, original column) keys, and exactly zero of them map to more than one harmonised term. So the label is a deterministic function of the input, and the function is printed in the paper - leakage by construction, confirmed independently in the sample table where only 3 of 308 input strings are ambiguous. The alternative labels are no better: the genetic ancestry calls in SRA are the output of Razi et al.'s model that predicts genotypes from RNA sequencing reads and then assigns continental groups, and the dbGaP ones are the output of NCBI's GrafPop program. Both are other models' predictions.

existing_models.name: Razi et al., 'Genotype prediction of 336,463 samples from public expression data' - a statistical model that calls genetic variants from RNA sequencing read counts and then assigns each sample a continental ancestry group
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported 99.5% overall genotype accuracy, 99.6% for the common allele and 90.4% for the rarer allele, applied to 315,443 human samples in recount3 with on average 932,460 variant sites called per bulk sample. I read only the search-result summary and abstract-level text, not the full paper, and I did not re-run anything. Its supplementary table of predicted labels and genetic principal components is public and is exactly what this paper imported.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved verbatim. A companion commentary ('Large-scale genotype prediction from RNA sequence data necessitates a new ethical and policy framework') frames the open problem as consent and privacy rather than accuracy, which I read only as a title and summary.

existing_models.name: GrafPop (Genetic Relationship And Fingerprinting), NCBI's ancestry-assignment program that dbGaP runs automatically on every submitted genotype set
existing_models.score_and_split: No accuracy number retrieved. I know of it only from this paper's Methods, which describe it computing genetic distances to reference populations and then applying fixed cutoffs to produce discrete groups such as European, African, South Asian, East Asian and two arbitrary 'Hispanic 1/2' bands.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved. This paper itself names the weakness: the cutoffs are arbitrary and the two Hispanic bands are ethnicity labels standing in for ancestry labels.

existing_models.name: MetaSRA (Bernstein et al., Bioinformatics 2017) - an automated pipeline that maps free-text Sequence Read Archive sample metadata onto biomedical ontology terms and classifies sample type
existing_models.score_and_split: No number retrieved; I read only search-result summaries and the abstract-level description. Pipeline code is at github.com/deweylab/MetaSRA-pipeline and the normalised database is downloadable in bulk. It covers tissue, cell type, disease and cell line - the same harmonisation job this paper did by hand for 968 tissue terms and 279 disease terms - but not population descriptors.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved verbatim; the stated motivation is that manual annotation of the archive is intractable at scale.

existing_models.name: Benchmarks of genetic-ancestry inference from single-cell RNA sequencing (2025) comparing nearest-centroid assignment on genetic principal components, a random forest on those components, and supervised ADMIXTURE
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported as giving accurate ancestry and admixture estimates despite imperfect variant calling from single-cell reads; I retrieved only the search-result summary and quote no number.

existing_models.name: RNAScope-Ancestry (2025) - a published pipeline that infers genetic ancestry and transcriptome features together from short-read RNA sequencing
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved as a title and summary only. Described as not beating genotyping arrays on variant resolution but useful because the RNA data already exists.

existing_models.name: A model that predicts which population descriptor a depositor will type, or which studies will omit one
existing_models.score_and_split: I found none in four searches, and searching is weak evidence, so call this likely absent. But the gap has an obvious cause rather than being an opportunity: the quantity is a human reporting habit, the published Table S4 dictionary already converts the strings with no ambiguity, and 97% of samples have no string at all to learn from.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: This paper's own discussion names the unsolved problem as a policy one - repositories need mandatory, structured population-descriptor fields - not a modelling one.

backbone.name: None of the checklist's biological backbones apply, because the deposit contains no sequences, no molecules, no structures and no expression matrices - only categorical metadata. The only backbone that would fit at all is a small open text encoder (for example PubMedBERT or SciBERT, biomedical language models with open weights on Hugging Face) applied to the free-text descriptor strings.
backbone.hardware: Central processing unit only, and trivially so: embedding 308 distinct short strings takes seconds, and even all 23,880 rows is a few minutes. The backbone is not the constraint; there is nothing worth embedding.
backbone.licence: Article CC BY-NC; code and the SRA metadata zip CC BY-NC 4.0; dbGaP_study_649.csv CC BY 4.0. The non-commercial clause on the data would restrict commercial reuse but not a learning project. PubMedBERT and SciBERT weights are permissive.

integration.partner_dataset: Razi et al.'s supplementary table of predicted continental ancestry labels and genetic principal components for 336,463 Sequence Read Archive runs, which is the partner this paper already used; secondarily recount3 itself (about 316,000 human RNA sequencing samples with uniformly processed expression) and MetaSRA's normalised metadata.
integration.join_key: BioSample accession (SAMN/SAME/SAMD) and SRA study accession, both present and clean in the 23,880-row table; the supplementary recoding tables also carry Cell Ontology, UBERON anatomy and Disease Ontology identifiers, which are proper standard identifiers.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does what a depositor wrote about their participants' ancestry agree with what their RNA sequencing data says, and can you predict from a study's visible features which depositors will get it wrong? The question is real and the identifiers are genuinely good, but the join is one-to-many (several sequencing runs per BioSample, which the authors resolved by picking one run at random), the overlap is only 3,176 samples by the paper's own count, and both sides of the comparison are machine-generated - one a published dictionary, the other another model's prediction - so the join cannot support a model even though it supported a nice figure.

controls.positive_control: Would be strong if the label were real: require the model to reproduce the Table S4 recoding on held-out strings, and require it to recover the paper's headline effect that United States institutions use racial terms while institutions elsewhere use geographic terms (Fisher odds ratio 6.03). The first control is also the project's death sentence - a 454-row dictionary passes it perfectly.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the harmonised label and confirm collapse to the majority class, which is already 12,538/16,797 non-missing rows labelled White; and hold out whole SRA studies rather than samples, since one study contributes up to 1,857 rows with an identical descriptor string and a random split would leak outright.
controls.external_validation: Genuinely good and cheap, which is the frustrating part. The manual literature review of 620 studies is an independent extraction of the same quantity from publications rather than metadata, and the paper reports the two agreeing fully in only one of 61 cases. A ReleaseDate column spanning 2012-2022 gives a free temporal split, and the dbGaP table is a second repository. The evaluation machinery is not the problem here; the label is.

honest_claim_h3: The most a model built on what is actually deposited could honestly claim is: 'given the free-text ancestry or race string a depositor typed into one of eight optional metadata fields, this reproduces the category two of the paper's authors assigned to that same string by hand, among the 3% of samples where anybody typed anything at all, drawn from 261 studies of which 62% came from United States institutions.' That is a statement about a 454-row lookup table, not about human diversity.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the free-text ancestry wording a scientist typed into a public database to predict the standard category a curator would assign it.
plain_idea.train_on: What the model would see: one short free-text string per sample, such as 'Caucasian', 'CAUC', 'Yellow race' or 'Asian (Nepali)', plus the depositing institution's country and the year. The table has 23,880 samples, but I counted only 308 distinct strings in it, from 261 studies - so 308 is the real number of examples.
plain_idea.predict: A harmonised category: either a United States Census race term (White, Black or African American, Asian, and so on) or a world region (Europe, East Asia, Subsaharan Africa, and so on). The true answer comes from two of the paper's authors reading each term and assigning it by hand, with the complete term-to-category mapping published as supplementary Table S4.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: The underlying goal is worth a lot - repository curators at NCBI and EBI, and anyone assembling a diverse RNA sequencing cohort, would love an automatic way to clean up these fields. But the paper has already published the complete mapping as a 454-row table, so the useful artefact exists and a model would only memorise it.

ml_idea: Three framings, and all three die on the files. (1) The task the deposit literally supports: classify a free-text population-descriptor string into a harmonised race or geography category. The table is clean - 23,880 rows, no duplicate BioSamples, documented harmonised columns - but I verified that the label is a deterministic recode of the input via the paper's own 454-row Table S4 (271 distinct keys, zero ambiguous), and that the 23,880 rows contain only 308 distinct input strings of which 3 are ambiguous. A dictionary beats any model, by construction, and the dictionary is already published. (2) The task the paper's most interesting figure invites: predict a donor's genetically inferred ancestry, or predict when the author-reported label disagrees with it. Here the label is another model's output - Razi et al.'s genotype-from-RNA-sequencing predictions, or NCBI's GrafPop cutoffs - the merged table was never deposited, the overlap is 3,176 samples by the paper's own count, and the inputs (actual expression data) are only accession numbers pointing at terabytes in recount3. (3) The meta-science task: predict from a study's visible features (journal, year, country, tissue, disease, sample size) whether it will report a population descriptor at all. This is the only framing with an honest label, and it is closest to a real question, but the unit is the study: 261 studies in the sample table, 620 in the manual review of which only about 61 report anything, and 649 in dbGaP - an order of magnitude short, with the outcome driven almost entirely by one feature (United States institution yes/no, Fisher odds ratio 6.03) that the paper has already measured. There are two small, genuinely useful findings to report back rather than model: the deposit's only sample-level table is a 2024-09-01 snapshot that disagrees with the published Table 1 (23,880 rows and 261 studies versus 23,803 and 244), and the files the analysis code actually reads (20250517_allSRAFinal.rds, 20250605_allSRAFilt_country.rds, from_Kasper_suppTable3.csv, final_bioproject_biosample_runlist.csv) are not in the deposit, so the published numbers cannot be reproduced; also the manual-review export is deposited under the literal filename 'C:\combinedRecount3.csv' and the supplementary spreadsheets' internal sheet names are mislabelled by one or two table numbers. That is a short note to the authors, not a project.

effort.compute_note: All numbers are from files I actually opened on this laptop: the four processed tables together are about 1.4 MB and loaded in under a second, so peak memory is dominated by the interpreter, not the data. embedding_hours assumes pushing 308 distinct short strings (or at most 23,880) through a small text encoder on the processor, which is seconds to minutes; nothing was timed. hours_to_feature_table reflects that the tables are already model-ready - the work is reading the undocumented column names, since the repository README is still the unedited GitLab template.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the distinct descriptor strings in the one sample-level table, then open supplementary Table S4. The answers are 308 distinct strings and a published 454-row lookup table with 271 keys and zero ambiguity, which means the label is the input passed through a dictionary the authors already give you. Fifteen minutes. The second-cheapest check is to count the studies: 261.

verdict_reason: This is a meta-science audit of metadata reporting, not a modelling dataset, and it fails Part A at five of the eight killers - all checked in the files, not inferred from the abstract. A2: nothing deposited is a measurement; every column is either a string a depositor typed or a category the authors assigned to that string, and the one target with a physical basis (a donor's genetic ancestry) is not here, so it would have to be constructed by re-merging Razi et al.'s separate table over a one-to-many run-to-sample join that the authors resolved by picking a run at random. A8 is the decisive one: I opened supplementary Table S4 and found a 454-row published dictionary with 271 distinct (term, column) keys and exactly zero ambiguous mappings, so the harmonised label is a deterministic function of the model's own input - and independently, in the 23,880-row sample table, only 3 of 308 distinct input strings map to more than one label. The alternative labels are other models' outputs (Razi et al.'s genotype prediction from RNA sequencing reads, NCBI's GrafPop cutoffs). A5 fails as effective sample size: 23,880 rows reduce to 308 distinct inputs from 261 studies, and the other tables are 649, 678, 324 and 120 rows. A3 fails for the only framing with a real measurement, because the expression data behind it exists here only as BioSample accession numbers pointing at terabytes in recount3. A7 fails mildly but informatively: the deposited sample table (23,880 rows, 261 studies) disagrees with the published Table 1 (23,803 samples, 244 studies), the Methods give a third set of numbers and Table S4's frequencies a fourth, and the intermediate files the analysis code actually reads were not deposited, so the published numbers cannot be reproduced from the release. To the authors' credit, A1, A4 and A6 pass cleanly - the deposit is fully open with no login or application (CC BY-NC 4.0 for the code and SRA zip, CC BY 4.0 for the dbGaP table), everything parsed on the first try, there are no duplicate BioSamples, and the whole modellable working set is about 1.4 MB. The evaluation machinery a project would want is also unusually good and cheap here: a ReleaseDate column for a temporal split, an independent manual literature review of 620 studies as external validation, and 261 studies to hold out. None of that rescues it, because the field is already served - MetaSRA does automated metadata harmonisation with open code, and Razi et al., GrafPop, RNAScope-Ancestry and the 2025 single-cell ancestry benchmarks all cover ancestry inference from RNA data - and because the paper's real contribution, the 454-row recoding dictionary plus the 968-term tissue and 279-term disease mappings, is the artefact a model would be trying to reproduce. Scoring stopped at Part A, so score_items is empty by design; the empty parts are not a judgement on B through J.
